introduction.text: The Colonna dell'Immacolata is a nineteenth‑century monument in Rome that commemorates the dogma of the Immaculate Conception and serves as a focal point for annual papal celebrations.

history.description: The Corinthian column was discovered on 17 September 1777 during construction of the monastery for the Benedictine Order of Santa Maria della Concezione in Campo Marzio.
The dogma of the Immaculate Conception was proclaimed ex cathedra by Pope Pius IX in 1854.
The column was designed by Luigi Poletti and commissioned by Ferdinand II of the Two Sicilies, and dedicated on 8 December 1857.
In 1922 a replica of the column was raised on the campus of the University of Saint Mary of the Lake in Mundelein, Illinois.
Since December 1953, pontiffs have visited the monument annually and offered a bouquet of flowers at the base of the column.
The column was erected by city firemen, who raised it on December 18.

design.description: The monument consists of a square marble base with four bas‑reliefs and statues of biblical figures at the corners, supporting a 11.8‑meter Cipollino marble column topped by a bronze statue of the Virgin Mary.

art.description: Four statues of Hebrew figures—King David, Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Moses—each accompanied by a Latin biblical verse, adorn the base of the column.
